title: Question 6
stem: A neutron decays by emitting a $\beta^-$ particle.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Complete the equation below for this decay.

$$^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow$$
hints: Hint 1: Think about what must stay the same on both sides of any nuclear decay - the total top numbers and the total bottom numbers balance separately.
Hint 2: Remember a neutron turning into a proton keeps the nucleon number at 1 but increases charge by 1, and check the symbols for a proton, a beta particle and an antineutrino.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Balance the nucleon numbers on top**
You have $^{1}_{0}n$ on the left, so the top number total is 1. The $\beta^{-}$ and $\bar{\nu}$ both have nucleon number 0, so the new nucleon must carry all of it. That gives top number 1 for the first product.

Step 2: **Balance the proton numbers (charge) at the bottom**
On the left the bottom number is 0. On the right the $\beta^{-}$ is $^{0}_{-1}$ and the $\bar{\nu}$ is $^{0}_{0}$. To make $0 = Z + (-1) + 0$, you need $Z = +1$. A nucleon with $A=1$, $Z=1$ is a proton, $^{1}_{1}p$.

Step 3: **Write the full balanced equation**
Putting it together: $$^{1}_{0}n \rightarrow ^{1}_{1}p + ^{0}_{-1}\beta^{-} + ^{0}_{0}\bar{\nu}$$ This shows charge, baryon number and lepton number are all conserved.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: State the name of the particle represented by the symbol $\bar{v}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the bar on top of the $\nu$ symbol - in particle physics this bar always means the antiparticle version, paired with the electron in beta decay.

enrichment.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the bar on top of the $\nu$ symbol - in particle physics this bar always means the antiparticle version, paired with the electron in beta decay.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: State the name of the class (group) of particles that includes $\beta^-$ and $\bar{v}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the two big families of matter particles - hadrons made of quarks, and the other family of fundamental particles that includes electrons and neutrinos and are not made of quarks.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort particles by family**
Electrons, muons, neutrinos and their antiparticles are not made of quarks and do not feel the strong force. They belong together in one fundamental family called leptons. Both the $\beta^{-}$ particle (an electron) and the $\bar{\nu}$ are leptons.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.text: the quark structure of the neutron,
hints: Hint 1: Recall that neutrons and protons are each made of three up and down quarks, and the neutron is neutral while the proton is +e - which combination gives zero net charge?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Build the neutron from quarks**
A down quark has charge $-1/3e$ and an up quark has charge $+2/3e$. To get total charge zero you need two downs and one up: $$-1/3 -1/3 +2/3 = 0$$ So a neutron is $ddu$.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: the change to the quark structure when the neutron decays.

markscheme_points.text: a down / d (quark) changes to an up / u (quark) or $ddu \rightarrow uud$

hints: Hint 1: Compare the starting neutron $ddu$ with the final proton from part (a) - which quark flavour must have changed to increase the charge from 0 to +1?
parts.proper_answer: a down quark changes to an up quark ($ddu \rightarrow uud$)
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See beta decay at quark level**
From (a) a neutron becomes a proton, and from (d)(i) a neutron is $ddu$ while a proton is $uud$. The only way to do this is for one $d$ quark with charge $-1/3e$ to change into a $u$ quark with charge $+2/3e$. That $+1e$ increase is carried away as the $\beta^{-}$ particle, with the antineutrino balancing energy and momentum.
